title: Lesson 40: Stateful vs Stateless Agents: Context, Memory, and Tool State
description: Why a language model remembers almost nothing and knows a great deal, and how context, memory, and tool state become the architecture that decides whether an agent is useful on day thirty.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Stateful vs Stateless Agents: Context, Memory, and Tool State”, a B2B support agent asks the same qualifying questions on every contact, and a correction an expert makes mid-call disappears when the call ends. What is the architectural fix?
options: Increase the context window so the entire conversation history can be resent on every request.
Move state behind the API boundary: the client sends a message plus a session identifier, and the agent loads the relevant state and writes the updated state back.
Fine-tune the model on the correction so it persists in the weights.
Add more tools so the agent can look up whatever it needs at answer time.
questions.explanation: A stateless design pushes context selection onto the client and loses every correction at the end of the call, so the fix is a durable state layer the server reads and writes.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Context is what survives beyond the window, and memory is what is in the window right now.
A stateful agent is one giant record, so all durable knowledge belongs in a single store.
Consolidation is optional, because searching a pile of raw transcripts is as trustworthy as searching a curated index.
Semantic memory holds domain facts, policies, and durable knowledge and answers what is true, while episodic memory records time-indexed experiences and answers what happened.
questions.explanation: Working, episodic, semantic, and procedural layers hold different lifetimes and costs, and consolidation is what keeps the durable store small enough to retrieve from well.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Because the attention budget is finite and recall degrades as context grows, an eviction and summarization strategy is non-negotiable, and tool output has to be designed for context efficiency.
Longer context always improves recall, so a model with a large window should be filled with as much history as possible.
Memory without grounding is safe as long as the store is durable.
One-shot extraction and classification tasks should be built stateful so they improve across requests.
questions.explanation: Context rot means longer context does not mean better recall, so something must always leave the window and the decision about what that is belongs to the architecture, not to the raw transcript.
